q1: SELECT f1.drinker, f2.drinker FROM (SELECT drinker, SUM(times_a_week) AS st FROM frequents GROUP BY drinker) AS f1, (SELECT drinker, SUM(times_a_week) AS st FROM frequents GROUP BY drinker) AS f2 WHERE f1.drinker < f2.drinker AND f1.st = f2.st
q2: SELECT DISTINCT a.drinker, b.drinker FROM Frequents AS a CROSS JOIN Frequents AS b WHERE a.drinker < b.drinker AND a.bar = b.bar AND a.times_a_week = b.times_a_week

Q1: It's taking two copies of the same subquery. The subquery groups the Frequents table by drinker and sums the times_a_week. Then it's doing a cross join between these two copies and selecting pairs where the drinker names are in order (f1.drinker < f2.drinker) and their total times_a_week sums are equal. So Q1 is finding pairs of drinkers who have the same total frequency across all bars.

Q2: This one does a cross join of the Frequents table with itself (a and b). It filters where a.drinker < b.drinker, and where a.bar equals b.bar and a.times_a_week equals b.times_a_week. So Q2 finds pairs of drinkers who have the same bar and same times_a_week for at least one bar entry. But since it's cross join, each row in a is paired with each row in b, so for each pair of drinkers, if they have any common (bar, times_a_week) entry, they'll appear in the result.

The key difference is that Q1 compares total sums across all bars, while Q2 compares individual entries (same bar and same times per week). So, two drinkers could have the same total sum (so they appear in Q1) but not have any overlapping bar and times entry (so they wouldn't appear in Q2). Conversely, two drinkers could have overlapping entries (so in Q2) but different total sums (so not in Q1).
